resources.string:
An ordinary blink: the model closes to 86% at most and leaves 3% after opening.
Eyes do not close fully → lower “Snap-shut line”.
Eyes look half-shut when open → raise “Snap-open line”.
Blinks feel sluggish → lower “Eye smoothing”.

Blink is processed per eye. First the ends snap: x′ = 0 when x < θ_low, x′ = 1 when x > θ_high, otherwise x′ = x; output x + s·(x′ − x), with θ_low < θ_high; this step does not depend on the source rate. Then adaptive smoothing: Reference share at 24 Hz α₀ = 1 − exp(−k·|x − y₋₁|), with x this input and y₋₁ the previous output; at runtime α = 1 − (1 − α₀)^r, r = Δt ÷ (1/24 s), y_α = y₋₁ + α·(x − y₋₁), output y = x + s·(y_α − x). A larger difference gives a larger share, so large movements follow fast and small jitter slowly. Example: with k = 9 a difference of 0.01 gives α₀ ≈ 8.6%, 0.1 gives α₀ ≈ 59.3%.

The eyes turn quickly to one side and stay, with small jitter in the model's value. The sooner green reaches the top, the more responsive the gaze; the flatter it stays, the steadier.
Gaze lags → raise “Eye small-movement speed” or lower “Eye smoothing”.
Gaze shakes while held → do the opposite.
Both settings also apply to blinks, squints and wide eyes.

LookDown, LookIn, LookOut, LookUp, Squint, Wide and Blink each use the same adaptive smoothing. Reference share at 24 Hz α₀ = 1 − exp(−k·|x − y₋₁|), with x this input and y₋₁ the previous output; at runtime α = 1 − (1 − α₀)^r, r = Δt ÷ (1/24 s), y_α = y₋₁ + α·(x − y₋₁), output y = x + s·(y_α − x). A larger difference gives a larger share, so large movements follow fast and small jitter slowly. Example: with k = 9 a difference of 0.01 gives α₀ ≈ 8.6%, 0.1 gives α₀ ≈ 59.3%.

The brows go up, stay for over a second, then come down. With stock settings they take about a second to get there, mostly because of “Extra brow steadying”.\nBrows lag behind → lower “Extra brow steadying” first; if still slow, raise “Brow speed”.\nBrows shake while held → do the opposite.

“Brow smoothing” is composite exponential smoothing on BrowDown, BrowInnerUp and BrowOuterUp: reference share at 24 Hz α₀ = w²·(1 − q·m), with w = “Brow speed”, q = “Hold brows during blinks” and m as on “Raise while blinking”; at runtime α = 1 − (1 − α₀)^r. Example: w = 0.6, m = 0 gives α₀ = 36%, about 11.2% per update at Δt = 1/90 s.\n“Extra brow steadying” is a 2-D Kalman filter on BrowInnerUp and BrowOuterUp with identity transition and observation, process noise Q (“Steadying speed”) and measurement noise R (“Steadying resistance”). Its steady-state gain K satisfies K²/(1 − K) = Q/R; Q = R gives K ≈ 61.8% at the 24 Hz reference, about 22.6% per update at Δt = 1/90 s. At runtime Q is adjusted by Δt so the steady-state response does not depend on the source rate. Both steps start from the previous final output, so together they are much slower.

The brows rise while the eyes blink once (blue dotted line). At the moment of a blink or eye turn the brows are held, so green starts later.\nBrows hardly move while you talk → lower “Hold brows during blinks”.\nWith a high “Extra brow steadying” the difference is small; lower it first to compare.

m ∈ [0, 1] is this eye\'s Blink change plus half the summed change of the four gaze directions, taken against the output about 83 ms earlier (at runtime the stored output nearest 2·Δt₀). “Brow smoothing” reference share α₀ = w²·(1 − q·m); with q = 100% and m = 1, α₀ = 0 and the brows do not move in that update. This only affects “Brow smoothing”; the Kalman filter of “Extra brow steadying” ignores m.

The model outputs a 50% raise (blue dotted line) and a 25% frown at once. Processing pushes the weaker frown down so the brows move one way.\nWorried looks that raise and frown together do not show → lower “Raise or frown, not both” or “Strictness”.

u is BrowInnerUp, d is BrowDown. They are redistributed by power weights: W_d = |d|^p ÷ (|u|^p + |d|^p + 10⁻¹⁰), d′ = W_d·(u + d); W_u likewise, u′ = W_u·(u + d′), using the processed d′. Output u + s·(u′ − u), and likewise for d. A larger p keeps only the stronger side: with u twice d, p = 4 gives weights 16:1, p = 2 gives 4:1. Computed independently each update, independent of the source rate.

Only the eyes open wide (blue dotted line); the brows themselves rise 10%. Stock settings add a large brow raise for wide eyes, so the avatar seems to lift its brows.\nWide eyes raise the brows too much → lower “Wide eyes lift brows” or “Wide-eye lift amount”.\nFor a more dramatic stare → raise them.

u is BrowInnerUp after the raise/frown step, v is this eye\'s Wide. u′ = u + g·v when u < θ, otherwise u′ = u; output u + s·(u′ − u), limited to [0, 1] before smoothing. The result also feeds the outer-brow link. Computed independently each update, independent of the source rate.

One blink (blue dotted line) with the brows at rest; the model\'s frown is only about 5%. Processing adds a frown while the eyes close, so the avatar lowers its brows on every blink.\nBrows twitch with blinks → lower “Closed eyes lower brows” or “Blink frown amount”.

d is BrowDown after the raise/frown step, b is this eye\'s Blink. d′ = d + g·b when d < θ, otherwise d′ = d; output d + s·(d′ − d), limited to [0, 1] before smoothing. g is dimensionless; θ, b and d are 0–1 action values. Computed independently each update, independent of the source rate.

Only the brow tails rise; the inner brows stay at 10% (blue dotted line). Processing pulls the tails back to the inner height, so with stock settings raising just the tails barely shows.\nFor brow tails that move on their own → lower “Outer brow follow”.
o is the model\'s BrowOuterUp, u′ is this eye\'s BrowInnerUp after the raise/frown step and the wide-eye link. Output o + s·(u′ − o). Each eye separately, independent of the source rate.

Four quick syllables open and close the jaw. The closer green follows grey, the more accurate the mouth; lower, later peaks mean too much smoothing.\nThe mouth barely opens while talking → lower “Jaw and smile extra smoothing” first; if not enough, lower “Mouth smoothing” or raise “Mouth small-movement speed”.\nLips jitter → do the opposite.

Adaptive exponential smoothing on the 32 mouth shapes other than TongueOut, as for the eyes: α₀ = 1 − exp(−k·|x − y₋₁|), converted by Δt, output y = x + s·(y_α − x).\nJawOpen, MouthSmile_L/R, MouthLeft and MouthRight use two passes: α₁ = 1 − exp(−k·|x − y₋₁|), v = y₋₁ + α₁·(x − y₋₁), α₂ = 1 − exp(−k·|v − y₋₁|), composite reference share α₀ = α₁·[(1 − s₂) + s₂·α₂], then converted by Δt. Both passes use the same previous output, so the share shrinks near the target.\nExample: k = 6, x = 0.3, y₋₁ = 0.2 gives α₁ ≈ 45.1%, α₂ ≈ 23.7%, composite about 10.7%. With s = 0 both passes are skipped.
Peak later than the model by

After talking the mouth closes, but the model still shows about 5% jaw opening. “Leftover removal” learns this value and subtracts it, so green should end near 0.\nThe avatar\'s mouth stays slightly open → raise “Leftover removal” or “Leftover range width”.\nThe mouth takes long to close → raise “Mouth small-movement speed” or lower “Jaw and smile extra smoothing”.

Each of the 32 shapes other than TongueOut learns an offset β: while |x − c| < h, β ← β + α·(x − β), with α converted from the 24 Hz reference learning weight w by Δt: α = 1 − (1 − w)^r. While |β| < L the output is x − s·β. JawOpen (mouth33 index 5) uses centre c₅, the others c. Default learning intervals: general (0, 0.04), JawOpen (0.02, 0.06); w = 50% gives a time constant of about 60 ms, independent of the source rate. With s = 0 subtraction stops but learning continues, and the learned MouthClose offset β₇ still feeds the lip closure addition.\nThe two-pass smoothing that follows takes a very small share when the difference is small, which is the slow tail in the chart.

After a smile the face relaxes, but the model still shows about 2.5% smile. This works as in “After closing the mouth”, except that shapes other than the jaw use “Leftover range centre (other shapes)”.\nThe avatar keeps smiling after you relax → raise “Leftover removal” or move the range centre to cover this value.
As in “After closing the mouth”, with general channels using centre c. MouthSmile_L/R are among the five two-pass shapes, so their return also has a slow tail.

With the mouth closed and relaxed, the model\'s lip closure (MouthClose) is only 1–2%. Processing always adds 8–9% so the lips look closed. Jaw opening (JawOpen) is a separate movement and is not affected.\nLips look pressed together → lower “Lip closure boost” or “Base boost”.\nLips part too far while talking → raise them.

Δ = s·min(β₇ ÷ d·a + b, c), added to MouthClose (mouth33 index 7). β₇ is the offset learned for this channel, see “After closing the mouth”; d, a, b and c are in action values. By default β₇ = 0 adds 0.08 and β₇ = 0.02 adds 0.09. These are model action values; how far the avatar\'s lips actually close depends on the PC-side mapping and the blendshapes. Independent of the source rate.

During a smile the model outputs a strong smile (blue dotted line) and a 12% dimple. Processing shrinks weaker shapes in proportion so the main shape stands out.\nSmall corner, dimple or nose movements disappear → lower “Shrink weak shapes” or raise “Keep weak shapes”.\nToo many small stray shapes → raise “Shrink weak shapes”.

Over the 33 mouth values of this update take the minimum L and maximum H; relative strength r = (x − L) ÷ (H − L + 10⁻¹⁰). Multiplier m = 1 + k·log₁₀(r + d), output x + s·(x·m − x), then limited to [0, 1]. m < 1 (shrink) when r + d < 1, enlarging above. Example: k = 0.6, d = 0.1 gives r = 0.1 × about 0.581, r = 0.5 × about 0.867, r = 1 × about 1.025. CheekPuff (index 0) counts for L and H but is not scaled itself. Independent of the source rate.
Stick the tongue out, then back
The tongue comes out, stays for a second, then goes back.\nThe tongue appears or retracts late → lower “Tongue smoothing” or raise “Tongue speed”.\nThe tongue flickers → do the opposite.

Exponential moving average (EMA): y = y₋₁ + α·(x − y₋₁). Follow speed w is the weight at the 24 Hz reference; at runtime α = 1 − (1 − w)^r, r = Δt ÷ (1/24 s). With w = 60%, 60% is taken per update at 24 Hz and about 21.7% at Δt = 1/90 s, both with a time constant of about 45 ms, independent of the source rate. Finally mixed by s: x + s·(y − x). The input is TongueOut after the threshold step.

The tongue comes out only a little, 45% from the model. Stock settings treat anything under 60% as no tongue, so the avatar shows nothing.\nA slight tongue does not show → lower “Tongue trigger line”.\nThe tongue flashes when you are not sticking it out → raise “Tongue trigger line”.

x is TongueOut after “Shrink weak shapes”. x′ = 0 when x < θ, x′ = g·x when x > θ, unchanged at x = θ; output x + s·(x′ − x), limited to [0, 1] before smoothing. Example: θ = 0.6, g = 1.5 turns 0.7 into 1.05, limited to 1. Independent of the source rate.
